items.title: USPTO Official Tribal Insignia Database Released Under FOIA
items.summary: This archive contains records released by the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) in response to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request seeking a digital copy of the agency’s database of official tribal insignias, along with copies of each official tribal insignia contained in the database as of the date of the request. In its July 16, 2026, response, the USPTO stated that it identified a responsive spreadsheet and released it in full, which is available below. The USPTO’s Native American Tribal Insignia Database is a component of the agency’s trademark search system. It exists to assist trademark examining attorneys in determining whether a pending trademark application falsely suggests a connection to the official insignia of a federally or state-recognized Native American tribe. The spreadsheet included in this release provides a snapshot of the USPTO’s official tribal insignia database at the time the FOIA request was processed. ### Document Archive FOIA Release Letter Tribal Database [119MB] The post USPTO Official Tribal Insignia Database Released Under FOIA first appeared on The Black Vault .

items.title: FOI lawsuits on origins of Covid-19,  gain-of-function research and biolabs
items.summary: U.S. Right to Know, a nonprofit newsroom and public health research group, has filed 46 lawsuits against federal and state agencies for violating Freedom of Information laws. The lawsuits are part of our efforts to uncover what is known about the origins of novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, leaks or mishaps at biosafety labs, and the risks of gain-of-function research that seeks to augment the infectivity or lethality of potential pandemic pathogens. We have filed 298 state, federal, and international public records requests seeking information about the origins of SARS-CoV-2, and the risks of biosafety labs and gain-of-function research. Read more about our findings so far , why we are conducting this investigation , recommended readings and documents we have obtained in our investigations. FOI lawsuits filed (46) U.S. Department of State : On August 18, 2026, USRTK filed a lawsuit against the State Department for violating provisions of the FOIA. The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, seeks cable traffic between the State Department and the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT Taipei) that relates to Taiwanese data or assessments about the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic. Case 3:26-cv-08558. (45) Department of Energy: On April 28, 2026, USRTK filed a lawsuit against the DOE for violating provisions of the FOIA. items.title: FBI Files: Historical Figures & Groups
items.summary: Background Welcome to the FBI Files on Historical Figures & Groups archive at The Black Vault. This comprehensive collection provides a unique lens into the lives and activities of various prominent individuals and groups that have played significant roles in shaping history. These files offer a rare glimpse into the FBI’s surveillance, investigation, and documentation of notable personalities and organizations, revealing the intricate ways they interacted with or were perceived by the U.S. government. From influential political leaders and activists to groundbreaking cultural figures, these documents span a wide spectrum of history and provide an invaluable resource for understanding the past. As you navigate through this archive, you will encounter a diverse array of FBI files, each telling a story that contributes to our understanding of historical events and figures. These files include detailed investigations, surveillance reports, and correspondences, all of which highlight the complex relationship between these figures and the federal agency. Whether you are a student, researcher, or history enthusiast, this archive serves as a fascinating portal into the past, offering insights into the motives, actions, and societal impacts of some of the most intriguing figures and groups in history. This collection is not just about the individuals and groups it covers, but also about the broader context of American history and the role of national security in it. Document Archive…

Often dubbed “Pennsylvania’s Roswell,” it involved reports of a fiery fireball streaking over several U.S. states and Canada, a crash in the woods near the village of Kecksburg, and an alleged military recovery of an unknown object [1] . Over the decades, the incident has been the subject of intense speculation – from meteor to secret Cold War satellite to extraterrestrial craft – and persistent efforts by investigators to unearth official records. items.title: The Pangram Paradox: The Problem with AI “Detecting” other AIs
items.summary: Op-ed: This is an opinion piece published on Unlimited Hangout . Most articles published on UH are not opinion pieces, so we are clearly labeling those that are. It should be no secret to readers of Unlimited Hangout that I have a very negative view of the impact that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is having on independent media and media in general. As someone who has been impersonated by AI daily on large video platforms for a few years now, I have come to acutely feel that AI is becoming a dangerous force that is making it increasingly difficult for well-meaning readers/viewers to distinguish between what is real and what is false. I don’t mean just for those hoping to view my content, as the personal issue I am facing is a microcosm of a much larger problem. As a result, one might think that I would have been pleased, if not relieved, to see Substack, a large platform for professional writers, partner with an “AI detection tool.” Not only am I not pleased, but I have now taken the time to write an opinion piece explaining why I think this is bad and to also explain where I think a lot of this is going. Substack’s new partner and, apparently, the AI detection tool of choice for most major media outlets right now is called Pangram. Pangram was founded in 2023, originally under the name Checkfor.ai, by Max Spero and Bradley Emi. Both Spero and Emi are Stanford graduates who, prior to Pangram, worked for companies like Nuro and Tesla where they both worked on AI self-driving…

items.title: Ralph Baric warned COVID statement could be used for ‘nefarious purposes to shift blame,’ email shows
items.summary: In early February 2020, as scientists and U.S. intelligence officials scrambled to understand the origins of the emerging coronavirus, prominent virologist Ralph Baric was asked to make a public statement knocking down claims that a chimeric coronavirus created in his University of North Carolina laboratory using genetic material supplied by a Wuhan scientist was the virus causing the outbreak. Baric thought the scientific answer was straightforward. The viruses differed by more than 5,000 nucleotides, the individual building blocks that make up a viral sequence, he wrote, adding the chimeric viruses created at his laboratory “were never sent to china.” But what appeared to worry him more was how his statement might be used. In a Feb. 6 email to a group of scientists who advise U.S. intelligence agencies, Baric said the requested statement could help rebut claims circulating on Chinese social media. But, he warned, it also could be used for “nefarious purposes to shift blame.” “I have received a few concerning, if not threatening, emails,” Baric wrote. He said he had informed his university and advised the group he “believe[d] that you should be informed as well.” The email, which was among records recently obtained by U.S. Right To Know, through an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, does not identify who asked Baric to make the statement, and it does not say whose blame he feared might be shifted, or onto…

Baric thought the scientific answer was straightforward. The viruses differed by more than 5,000 nucleotides, the individual building blocks that make up a viral sequence, he wrote, adding the chimeric viruses created at his laboratory “were never sent to china.” But what appeared to worry him more was how his statement might be used. In a Feb. 6 email to a group of scientists who advise U.S. intelligence agencies, Baric said the requested statement could help rebut claims circulating on Chinese social media. But, he warned, it also could be used for “nefarious purposes to shift blame.” “I have received a few concerning, if not threatening, emails,” Baric wrote. He said he had informed his university and advised the group he “believe[d] that you should be informed as well.” The email, which was among records recently obtained by U.S. Right To Know, through an ongoing Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, does not identify who asked Baric to make the statement, and it does not say whose blame he feared might be shifted, or onto…
